name: extension-object
intent: Extend the interface of individual objects at runtime, not their class: keep the key abstraction's interface stable and closed, attach each client-specific capability - interface plus its own state - as a separate extension object, and let clients query the subject for it by a stable id and handle its absence explicitly.
problem: One key abstraction serves several clients or subsystems that each need their own view of it, and the set of views is open-ended. Folding every client-specific operation and its state into the class bloats its interface, couples unrelated clients to one another, and forces a new subclass for every capability somebody might need - a subclass explosion that is static (it must exist at compile time) and permanent (each variant inherits the whole hierarchy).
context: Object-oriented designs built around a stable, widely shared key abstraction - a document component, a resource, a framework object, a service instance - whose client-specific capabilities cannot all be anticipated. It applies when the capability must be attachable to a single instance at runtime, when clients that do not need it must be unaffected by it, and when the class cannot simply be edited (third-party or sealed type, binary compatibility, or a variant per combination of features).
benefits: The key abstraction stays closed and stable: new client-specific interfaces arrive as extensions instead of edits to the class, its interface or its subclasses.
No bloated interfaces: a client that never uses a capability is not coupled to it, is not recompiled by it, and is not forced to implement or ignore empty operations.
The capability set is open-ended and per instance: extensions can be attached, replaced or removed on one object at runtime, instead of multiplying subclasses for each combination.

Each subsystem models its own role of the abstraction: its state and behaviour live in the extension object, so the key abstraction carries no fields for consumers it does not know about and one subsystem's changes cannot affect another's.
Extensions can be contributed by the team or plug-in that owns the concern, including after deployment (demand-loaded implementations), so the core stays independent of client teams.

The lookup is explicit: a client asks for the capability it wants and gets an answer about its presence, which is more predictable than downcasting the subject and hoping the concrete type happens to be the rich one.
tradeoffs: Clients become more complex: every use site must query for the extension, test for absence and choose a fallback path, so control flow grows around what used to be a direct call (Gamma lists this as a consequence, not an accident).

Extension identity has to be established by something: a string registry needs a namespace discipline, while a typeid/class token forces the client to reference the extension interface - either way the join happens at runtime and the compiler cannot check that the capability exists.

Lifetime and ownership must be decided explicitly wherever there is no garbage collector: the subject hands out references to extensions it does not control, so the options are subject-owns-extension with destruction, reference counting, or a documented borrow - and the extension usually has to be notified before its subject dies.
Demand loading adds a failure mode of its own: if the implementation of an extension is unavailable, the state attached to it must be preserved, or data is lost until the implementation returns.

Object schizophrenia: an extension's logical this is the subject while its physical this is the extension object, so extension code that operates on itself rather than routing through the subject silently works on the wrong identity.

Cost: an extension table per subject plus an indirection per access, which defeats inlining and cache locality in hot loops and data-oriented layouts - paid for a capability that may be absent anyway.

Abuse pressure: once the extension point exists, every new requirement is tempted to travel through it, and concepts that should have been modelled explicitly become invisible attached properties (Gamma's warning that extensions must stay the exception).

Static tooling cannot see the interface: refactoring, null analysis, remoting/serialization and generated API documentation all miss the attached capability, so the contract lives in convention and tests rather than in the type system.

participants.responsibility: Defines the identity of the key abstraction and declares the protocol for querying (and usually attaching) extensions; in the simplest case an extension is identified by a string, otherwise by an interface id or type token.
Implements the extension protocol for a concrete key abstraction: keeps the extensions it supports and returns the matching extension object, or an explicit absence, when a client asks.

Common base of all extensions: holds the reference to the subject it belongs to and carries the support needed to manage the extension itself (typically a notification before it or its subject is deleted).
Declares the interface for one specific extension, i.e. the capability the client depends on; it is what the client asks the subject for.
Implements that interface for a particular kind of subject and stores the state belonging to that capability, reading and writing it through the subject reference it owns.

Maps extension identity to extension instance and decides which extension is created for a subject (a per-subject dictionary, an adapter-factory registry, or a collection type - Gamma's dictionary variation, Microsoft's ExtensionCollection, Eclipse's IAdapterManager).
Asks the subject for the capability it needs and uses the returned extension only if it is present; it must handle absence rather than assume support.

use_cases: Compound document editors: a spelling checker enumerates the words of components through a TextAccessor extension that text components offer, while components without text simply cannot be asked for it (Gamma's motivating example from OpenDoc/OLE compound documents).

IDE and plug-in platforms: Eclipse's IAdaptable.getAdapter lets any object be adapted to a capability such as IPropertySource or ImageProvider that third-party plug-ins define, with adapter factories registered declaratively via the org.eclipse.core.runtime.adapters extension point — the canonical industrial instance, cited by Gamma himself.

VSCode extension API: extensions export typed APIs (T) via activate() and other extensions discover them via vscode.extensions.getExtension<publisher.name>(), creating an Extension Object registry per installation with lazy activation and lifecycle management.

.NET MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework): Export<T> and Import<T> decorators build a composition container that acts as an extension registry, discovering implementations of contracts (extension interfaces) across assemblies without static linkage.

UI frameworks: WPF attached properties let a parent (a layout panel, a data template) store values on any element of a foreign class hierarchy without deriving from the element's class — DockPanel.Dock and Grid.Column are canonical examples — and the value is per-element, not per-class.

COM QueryInterface: Microsoft's Component Object Model uses IUnknown::QueryInterface as a type-keyed extension lookup, returning an explicit interface pointer or E_NOINTERFACE — the binary-standard form of the pattern that inspired Gamma's treatment.

Third-party, sealed or generated types that must be enriched: attached validation rules, display metadata, or per-tenant configuration for a class whose source cannot be changed and which cannot be subclassed.

Fixed object models such as the DOM, where Node.setUserData/getUserData attach application data to nodes of a tree the application does not own, keyed by a name and released with a handler when the node is replaced.

TypeScript declaration merging: module augmentation adds namespaced properties to existing interfaces at compile time, effectively attaching an extension object whose shape is merged into the original declaration — used by tsconfig paths, router libraries, and Redux store types.

.NET extender providers: ToolTip, ErrorProvider and HelpProvider implement IExtenderProvider and contribute extender properties (ToolTip.ToolTip, HelpProvider.HelpString) to any control in the container; CanExtend(object) decides which targets qualify, so the per-control values live on the provider rather than on the control's class.

IntelliJ Platform: core model objects (VirtualFile, PsiElement, Project) implement UserDataHolder, and plugins attach per-instance state through type-safe Key<T> tokens created once into static fields — MY_KEY.set(holder, v) / MY_KEY.get(holder) — garbage-collected with the holder instead of tracked in side maps.
avoid_when: The set of capabilities is known up front and closed: declare them on the interface (or select among them with Strategy) instead - the extension machinery buys flexibility you will never use.

Clients need the guarantee that a capability is present: use a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive matching (or a proper interface) and let the compiler prove coverage, rather than returning null at runtime.
The interface should stay fixed and behaviour merely be augmented per instance: Decorator wraps the same interface, keeps every client unchanged and stacks several decorations reliably.
The object is a value with equality and copy semantics (the value scope): attached state has no identity to hang on, and copying or comparing the value would silently duplicate or drop it.
The capability is really a separate collaborator rather than an attribute of this object: model and inject it explicitly (Dependency Injection) instead of parking it in an extension table.

Your platform already runs a registry for exactly this purpose (Eclipse adapter factories, WCF extension collections, WPF attached properties): register there instead of building a parallel mechanism that clients will never discover.
anti_patterns: The untyped extension bag: a Map<String, Object> (a dict, a symbol table, a list of dynamic properties) attached to every object in the system, so nothing documents which extensions exist and every access ends in a cast.

Using extensions for concepts that belong in the design: stable, known requirements are attached dynamically, hiding them from the type system, the documentation and the tests — the abuse Gamma warns against explicitly.
One extension instance shared by many subjects, or a registry keyed by class instead of by instance: per-subject state cross-talks and the first concurrent access corrupts both subjects.
getExtension as a service locator: the registry grows into an ambient container resolving arbitrary dependencies, turning every lookup into an untraceable coupling that outlasts its original purpose.
Treating the absent branch as an error path that is never tested: on real object populations most subjects do not support most extensions, so absence is the normal case and must be exercised.

Object schizophrenia in delegation: an extension that calls a method on itself (this.someMethod()) instead of routing through the subject reference silently operates on the wrong identity — the physical extension rather than the logical subject.

State stored in the extension that is lost when the extension cannot be loaded: demand-loading scenarios that silently drop per-instance state when the DLL is unavailable rather than preserving it separately.

No conflict policy for extension registration: multiple plugins providing the same extension interface without a replacement or priority rule, so behaviour becomes non-deterministic depending on load order.
Monkey patching used as an architecture substitute: setattr on arbitrary objects instead of named extension contracts — undiscoverable by tooling, un-type-checkable, and fragile under refactoring.
Ignoring security boundaries: loading third-party extensions executes code; treating plugin registration as data rather than code execution exposes the host to malicious extensions.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: the key abstraction is closed for modification and open for extension through new extension types.
Interface segregation: a client depends only on the interface it actually uses, not on the union of every client's needs.
Composition over inheritance: capabilities are composed onto instances at runtime instead of multiplying subclasses.
Single responsibility: each extension encapsulates one client-specific concern, including the state that belongs to that concern.
Information hiding: extensions reach the subject through its key abstraction and a back-reference, rather than clients manipulating the subject's internals.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on an AbstractExtension interface and on a lookup contract, not on a concrete subject class.
best_practices: Keep every extension interface narrow and role-specific (one capability, named from the client's point of view) so clients depend on the smallest contract that serves them.
Return absence explicitly (null, nil, Optional, None) and make callers handle it; a capability that must always be present is a member, not an extension.

Identify extensions with a stable, collision-proof token — an interface id, a type token, a class object or a namespaced registry key — rather than a free-form string, and centralise that convention in one place.
Use generic typed lookups where available (getAdapter<T>() in Eclipse, vscode.extensions.getExtension<T>() in VSCode) to eliminate manual casting and make the contract explicit in the type system.
Centralise extension registration through a registry or adapter manager so clients can discover capabilities uniformly rather than each subject implementing its own lookup logic.

Decide and document the lifetime rule: who owns the extension, when it is removed, and how it is notified before the subject is destroyed; in non-GC languages prefer reference counting or explicit teardown over borrowing.
Give the extension a reference to its subject and perform every operation through it, so per-subject data is read from the subject and the extension machinery stays reusable.
Restrict who may attach: the registry is a capability store, so attaching must not be driven by untrusted input, and an extension lookup must never serve as an authorisation decision.
Document the extensions a subject supports as part of its public contract and test both branches — capability present and capability absent.
Cache the result of a lookup outside hot loops; extension access is an indirect function call that defeats inlining and may allocate on each query.
For plugin/extension ecosystems, define a version field on the exported API contract and validate it before calling — the provider may have loaded before the consumer initialised.
In Python, prefer protocols (typing.Protocol) to define extension contracts so type checkers can validate implementations without inheritance coupling.

Watch for service-locator drift: the extension registry is for capabilities of the host object, not a general-purpose dependency container — when everything starts asking the registry for unrelated dependencies, it has become a service locator.
sources: Erich Gamma, "Extension Object", in Robert C. Martin, Dirk Riehle & Frank Buschmann (eds), Pattern Languages of Program Design 3, Addison-Wesley, 1997, pp. 79-88 (the pattern's originating catalogue).
Erich Gamma & Richard Helm, "Designing Objects for Extensions", Dr. Dobbs SourceBook, #236, May/June 1995 (earlier version of the pattern).

Douglas C. Schmidt, "Extension Interface", in same volume as above — a related POSA pattern that distinguishes the Extension Object variant from the Distributed Extension Interface variant used in COM/CORBA; available at https://www.laputan.org/pub/sag/extension-interface.pdf.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_schizophrenia — coined by William Harrison, IBM Research, 1997; a key liability of delegation-based patterns including Extension Object.
https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/python/structural-patterns/extension-object-pattern/ — Python-specific implementation guidance, registry patterns, and service-locator drift warnings.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.componentmodel.iextenderprovider — Microsoft's extender-provider mechanism: ToolTip, ErrorProvider and HelpProvider attach per-component properties to foreign classes via CanExtend, the Windows Forms realisation of Extension Object.

https://plugins.jetbrains.com/docs/intellij/virtual-file.html — IntelliJ Platform Plugin SDK: VirtualFile implements UserDataHolder, the type-safe Key<T> extension-attachment facility every platform model object exposes.

https://www.freelikeapuppy.tech/post/extension-objects-there-s-nothing-to-like — practitioner critique of extension objects (Salesforce Nonprofit/Education Cloud): attached data standing in for first-class modelling degrades tooling, reporting and governance.

related_patterns_notes.extension-interface: the broader POSA pattern family; Extension Object is the in-process variant where the component itself returns interface references; the sibling Distributed Extension Interface variant uses proxies and factories for cross-address-space or cross-language scenarios (COM, CORBA).
related_patterns_notes.role-object: closely related; models different roles of the same abstraction as separate objects attached to a core; unlike Extension Object, role-object merges all roles into one physical identity, avoiding the object-schizophrenia problem at the cost of static role composition (GenVoca/Beta).
related_patterns_notes.type-object: disciplines subclassing by making the variant itself an object; used when the set of subtypes is open but the variation is in classification rather than per-instance attached capability.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: wraps the same interface the subject exposes, stacking transparently on top; clients remain unchanged. Extension Object adds a new interface the subject does not have and that the client must explicitly query for. Use Decorator when all clients should see the capability; use Extension Object when only some clients need it.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: encapsulates one interchangeable algorithm behind a stable interface and swaps it at runtime within a single context. Extension Object adds new interfaces with their own state and behaviour. Strategy answers 'how should this one thing be done?'; Extension Object answers 'what additional views of this thing are available?
related_patterns_notes.visitor: uses double dispatch to apply n operations across m element types in a fixed hierarchy without modifying the elements. Extension Object adds new interfaces to a single subject. Visitor is closed for new element types but open for new operations; Extension Object is open for new interfaces but requires explicit per-subject registration.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: converts the interface a subject already exposes into a different interface the client expects. Extension Object adds an entirely new interface the subject does not expose at all. Adapter is a conversion around an existing contract; Extension Object is an augmentation of the subject's capability surface.
related_patterns_notes.composite: structures objects recursively as 1-to-many hierarchies; decorators chain along a single delegatee. Extension Object does not imply hierarchy or chaining — each extension is an independent per-instance attachment with no implied delegation chain.
related_patterns_notes.mixin: merges capabilities statically into a class hierarchy at compile time; all mixed-in behaviour becomes part of the class identity. Extension Object attaches behaviour dynamically at runtime with per-instance state and no compile-time coupling. Mixins cannot represent per-instance optional roles; Extension Object can.
related_patterns_notes.capability-query: a general category of patterns that test for the presence of a capability before use; the extension lookup is one implementation of this query pattern.
